blocks.text: Imagine you have a bookshelf where each book is numbered and you can quickly find any book by its number. This is similar to how arrays work in programming.

blocks.markdown: Arrays and lists are fundamental data structures used to store sequences of elements. They allow efficient access and manipulation of data by using indices. In this lesson, we will explore the differences between arrays and lists, their operations, and the cost associated with these operations.

blocks.title: Array
blocks.text: An array is a collection of elements identified by index or key, where each element is of the same data type. Arrays have a fixed size.

blocks.title: List
blocks.text: A list is a collection of elements that can grow or shrink in size. Lists are more flexible than arrays and can contain elements of different data types.

blocks.markdown: Arrays provide constant-time access to elements using an index, which is denoted as $O(1)$. This means that accessing any element in an array takes the same amount of time, regardless of its position.

blocks.caption: Accessing the i-th element of an array A.

blocks.title: Accessing an Element in an Array
blocks.prompt: Consider an array `A = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]`. Access the third element.

steps.text: Identify the index of the third element. In programming, indices start at 0.
The third element is at index 2, so A[2] is the element we need.

blocks.markdown: Lists, unlike arrays, can dynamically resize. This flexibility comes with a trade-off in performance. While accessing an element is still $O(1)$, appending an element can be $O(1)$ on average, but inserting or removing elements can be more costly.

blocks.caption: Comparison of operation costs for arrays and lists.

blocks.title: Appending to a List
blocks.prompt: Append the number 60 to the list `L = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]`.

steps.text: Identify the current size of the list. The list has 5 elements.
Add the new element 60 to the end of the list.

blocks.markdown: A growable array, such as a list in Python, achieves amortized constant-time append by occasionally resizing itself. When the array is full, it allocates a larger block of memory and copies the existing elements to the new block. This resizing operation is costly, but it happens infrequently enough that the average cost per append remains constant.

blocks.title: Amortized Analysis
blocks.text: Amortized analysis considers the average time per operation over a sequence of operations, smoothing out costly operations that occur infrequently.

points: Arrays provide constant-time access but have a fixed size.
Lists are dynamic and can grow, but some operations may be costly.
Amortized analysis helps understand the average cost of operations like append.
